clue.text: Unenthusiastic old learner joining company

indicators.note: the old learner joins on after the company, so the pieces sit side by side

parts.note: CO is the standard abbreviation for company
O = old, as in O.E. for Old English
L = learner, from the L-plate on a learner driver's car

explanation.surface: A bored older student has just been taken on by a firm.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads old learner first, but the company comes first in the answer: 'joining' lets the pieces go in either order.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a cool reception is lukewarm, showing little interest.

clue.text: Break in children's game

definitions.meaning: to break with a sudden crack, as a twig does
a card game where players shout the name when two matching cards turn up

explanation.surface: A pause in the middle of a children's game.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Break' reads as a noun, an interval, but it is the verb: to snap a stick. Snap is also the matching card game.
explanation.definitionFit: Snap means break, and Snap is a card game played by children.

clue.text: Empty shores in which you'll see bird moves quickly

indicators.note: the bird is seen inside the emptied shores
emptying 'shores' removes everything but its outside letters

parts.note: SHORES with its inside emptied out leaves S…S
the coot is a black water bird

explanation.surface: Deserted beaches where a bird can be seen darting about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Moves quickly' is a verb in the third person, so the answer ends in S; the bird is a common crossword coot.
explanation.definitionFit: To scoot is to move quickly, so 'scoots' matches 'moves quickly'.

clue.text: Cleared off, say

indicators.note: 'off' as in gone off: the letters of 'cleared' have gone wrong

explanation.surface: Someone left in a hurry, so to speak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cleared off' reads as one phrase meaning ran away; split it, and 'off' is working on 'cleared'.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: declaring is stating out loud, which is what 'say' means as a verb.

clue.text: Bewildered prisoner must be integrated

explanation.surface: A baffled inmate has to be brought back into society.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Integrated' reads as rejoining society; it is the plainer sense of things fused into one piece.
explanation.definitionFit: Confused and bewildered both mean unable to think clearly.

clue.text: Movement offering stupid proposal at meeting?

parts.note: a motion is a proposal put to a meeting

explanation.surface: A political campaign that puts a foolish idea to a committee.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Movement' looks like a campaign group, which fits the meeting; it is literal moving about.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the physical sense: the power or act of moving from place to place.

clue.text: Good engineers finally made home most eco-friendly

parts.note: RE = Royal Engineers, the British Army's engineering corps

indicators.note: 'finally made' asks for the last letter of 'made'

explanation.surface: Skilled engineers have at last built the most environmentally sound house.
explanation.walkthrough: RE, the Royal Engineers, is the usual crossword meaning of 'engineers'; 'good' is just G.
explanation.definitionFit: Green means environmentally friendly, so greenest is the most eco-friendly.

clue.text: Coastal road — gosh, a suitable place!

parts.note: cor is a British exclamation of surprise, like gosh
a niche is a place that suits you exactly

explanation.surface: Someone driving along the seafront exclaims that this is just the spot.
explanation.walkthrough: COR is informal British for 'gosh' or 'wow'.
explanation.definitionFit: A corniche is a road cut along a coast or cliff face.

clue.text: Seaman conceals grim smells

indicators.note: the seaman holds the grim word hidden inside him

explanation.surface: A sailor is hiding some nasty whiffs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smells' could be a verb, but the grim sailor is hiding nouns: the smells themselves.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, in the British spelling with -OUR; 'grim' hints these are unpleasant ones.

clue.text: City serving beer and fancy pop

indicators.note: a fancy version of 'pop' is a fanciful rearrangement of its letters

explanation.surface: A town whose bars offer beer and exotic soft drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fancy pop' looks like a posh fizzy drink, but 'fancy' is shaking up the letters of POP.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by category: one of the largest cities in Syria.

clue.text: Bird seen in the museum

indicators.note: the bird can be seen inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: A stuffed bird on display at the museum.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs across the gap between two words, which is why 'the' is there.
explanation.definitionFit: The emu is a large flightless Australian bird.

clue.text: Remaining socialist, a maiden maybe

parts.note: socialists are on the political left
a maiden over is an example of an over

explanation.surface: A young unmarried woman stays true to her socialist politics.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket an over is a set of six balls, and a maiden is an over in which no runs are scored; 'maybe' flags it as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: Left over means remaining, as with food not eaten.

clue.text: Meal with starters for the English academy

indicators.note: the starters of each word are their first letters

explanation.surface: A dinner of several courses served at an English college.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Starters' belongs to the meal picture, courses before the main, but here it means first letters.
explanation.definitionFit: In Britain tea can be an evening or afternoon meal, not only the drink.

clue.text: Reasons chartered accountant employs

explanation.surface: Why an accountancy firm takes people on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reasons' reads like a verb (the accountant reasons), but it is a plural noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Causes are reasons why something happens.

clue.text: Bad person about to be given notice

parts.note: C = circa, Latin for about, used with dates
an ad is a notice in a paper

explanation.surface: A scoundrel who is on the point of being sacked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About to be given notice' reads as one phrase, soon to be fired; split it, and 'about' and 'notice' each give letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A cad is an old-fashioned word for a man who behaves dishonourably.

clue.text: Smashing fellow deemed mad is lying in grass

indicators.note: the fellow lies inside the word for grass

parts.note: to grass or sing is to inform to the police
'mad as a hatter', and the Mad Hatter of Alice in Wonderland

explanation.surface: A great bloke, thought crazy, stretched out on the lawn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grass' is the lawn in the picture, but it is British slang for informing, and so is 'sing'.
explanation.definitionFit: Smashing and shattering both mean breaking into pieces.

clue.text: Returned to stock to be brought back to tip-top condition?

definitions.meaning: put back into store: RE- plus a word for kept in stock
the sense used of an old building or painting repaired to its original state

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the first reading: split RE-STORED and it means put back into store.
explanation.definitionFit: Restored means brought back to good condition, and re-stored means put back into storage.

clue.text: Dad — sort to get involved with decrepit oldies

indicators.note: the two words get tangled up with each other

explanation.surface: Father is told to go and help some frail old people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sort' tempts as the anagram indicator, but it is fodder alongside 'Dad'.
explanation.definitionFit: A dotard is an old person grown feeble-minded.

clue.text: A hero apt to look silly in special headgear

indicators.note: the letters are made to look silly by being jumbled

explanation.surface: A hero likely to look ridiculous in a fancy hat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Special' is part of the definition, not the anagram indicator: an opera hat is a particular kind of hat.
explanation.definitionFit: An opera hat is a collapsible top hat, a special piece of headgear.

clue.text: Bad gent and I get into trouble arguing?

indicators.note: letters in trouble are in disorder

explanation.surface: A villain and I end up in hot water after quarrelling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bad' looks like the anagram indicator, but it is part of the fodder; the indicator is 'get into trouble'.
explanation.definitionFit: Debating is arguing a point, as in a formal debate.

clue.text: Did acts misguidedly for fans

indicators.note: the letters are put together the wrong way

explanation.surface: Performers put on ill-judged shows for their followers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fans' is not a verb here: addicts of something are its devoted fans.
explanation.definitionFit: A loose synonym: keen devotees of a hobby get called addicts, as in jazz addicts.

clue.text: Understand sound of the waves?

indicators.note: we want what a word sounds like, not how it is spelt

parts.note: the waves stand for the sea

explanation.surface: Grasping what the surf is saying.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound of the waves' reads as the noise of the surf; it is the word 'sea' said out loud.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom: 'I see' is what we say once something has sunk in.

clue.text: Fish dish ultimately going wrong

indicators.note: 'dish ultimately' is the last letter of 'dish'

explanation.surface: A fish recipe that ends up a failure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fish dish' looks like the definition, but 'dish' goes into the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by category: a common North Atlantic food fish.

clue.text: Serve as a piece of furniture, somehow not the best?

parts.note: to serve as something is to be it
a table is a piece of furniture

explanation.surface: Something is pressed into use as furniture, though it is not ideal.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is loose, as the question mark admits: whatever can be beaten is not the best.
explanation.definitionFit: Beatable describes something that can be beaten, so it cannot be the best.

clue.text: Fellow needing time to run

parts.note: an age is a period of time

explanation.surface: A chap who needs a moment before he can set off running.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Run' suggests jogging, but it means run a business.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the business sense: whoever runs a shop is in charge of it.

clue.text: Spy on street is Harry

parts.note: a mole is a spy planted inside an organisation

explanation.surface: The spy living on this road turns out to be someone called Harry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Harry' looks like a name; it is the verb, to harass.
explanation.definitionFit: An older sense: the word once meant simply to pester or harass, which is what harry means.

clue.text: Cockney worker is a joiner

indicators.note: Cockneys famously drop the H at the start of words

parts.note: a hand is a worker, as in farmhand

explanation.surface: A London labourer turns out to be a carpenter.
explanation.walkthrough: A Cockney is a working-class Londoner, whose accent drops the H: 'and' for 'hand'. 'Joiner' is a carpenter in Britain, but here it means a joining word.
explanation.definitionFit: 'And' is a conjunction, a word that joins others.

clue.text: Port in endless disorder

indicators.note: the disorder loses its end letter

explanation.surface: A harbour town caught up in continual unrest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Endless' reads as never-ending unrest, but it cuts the last letter off the disorder.
explanation.definitionFit: Rio de Janeiro is a major Brazilian port.

clue.text: Scottish island to the west with rocky hill — one offers an account

indicators.note: in an across answer, going west means reading right to left

parts.note: Arran is an island in the Firth of Clyde
a tor is a rocky hilltop, as on Dartmoor

explanation.surface: A storyteller describes the Scottish island and a craggy hill beyond it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To the west' reads as a direction on the map; in an across clue it means write the island backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A narrator is someone who gives an account of events.

clue.text: Female endlessly angry about problem with tights?

indicators.note: the female loses her last letter
'angry about' turns the angry word round

parts.note: red = angry, as in seeing red

explanation.surface: A woman is furious about something wrong with her tights.
explanation.walkthrough: A ladder is the British word for a run in tights or stockings.
explanation.definitionFit: A ladder is a vertical line of broken stitches in tights.

clue.text: Doctor getting minimal amount of money as ineffectual person

indicators.note: the doctor gets the money added on after him

parts.note: 1p, one penny, read as the letters IP

explanation.surface: A doctor earning next to nothing is seen as a weakling.
explanation.walkthrough: The smallest British coin is the penny, written 1p; the digit 1 stands in for the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: Informal British slang for a feeble, spineless or boring person.

clue.text: Language of poetry beginning to wither away

indicators.note: the poetry's first letter withers away

explanation.surface: The language of poems is starting to fade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beginning to wither' tempts as the W of wither; the whole phrase says the beginning withers away.
explanation.definitionFit: Erse is an old name for the Gaelic language of Scotland or Ireland.

clue.text: Minister in speech — one firing off?

indicators.note: the minister's title as spoken, not as spelt

parts.note: a canon is a clergyman attached to a cathedral

explanation.surface: A clergyman in the middle of a sermon who is sounding off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Firing off' suggests a ranting preacher; it is a gun firing.
explanation.definitionFit: A cannon is a big gun, something that fires off shots.

clue.text: Titaness turning out to be most unpleasant

indicators.note: the letters of Titaness are turned out into a new order

explanation.surface: A female Titan of Greek myth proves to be the worst of them all.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turning out to be' reads as 'proving to be'; the letters of TITANESS are what turn out.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: nasty means unpleasant, and -EST makes it the superlative.
